In the town of Satara, everyone knew the Jadhav family ran the fertiliser shop, and that Damini, the eldest, would take it over after her BCom.

Bilal had grown up in Lyon going to the mosque every Friday with his father, never missing. At twenty, at university, he started reading philosophy and asking questions he couldn't answer.
He told his father he wanted time to think about what he really believed.
His father's face closed. "After everything we gave you, you want to throw it away? You're lost."
Bilal walked back to his student room feeling like a traitor. He still loved the Friday meals, his father's voice reciting. He wasn't rejecting them. He just wanted his faith, or whatever it became, to be his own.
His friend Gabriel found him on the stairs. "You look awful."
"My dad thinks I've abandoned him."
"Have you?"
"No," Bilal said, and realised he meant it. "I just need to find out what's mine."

qa.a: He started reading philosophy.

qa.a: He felt guilty, like a traitor, and lonely, even though he still loved his father and the Friday meals.

Last year, at twenty-five, I, Vaibhav, woke up in my Pune office and realised I was living someone else's plan. Engineering because my father said so. This company because my uncle knew the manager.
My first instinct was to quit and blame everyone. I wrote an angry email to my father and deleted it.
My sister Rashmi said, "What do you actually want to keep?"
I made two lists. Keep: problem-solving, the friends I've made, supporting my parents. Drop: the parts of the job I only do to please others.
So I've started small. I moved to the product design team. I do a weekend course in user research.
When I told my father, I thanked him first. Then I explained. He listened. That surprised me most.

Avni and Keerthana had been best friends since Class 2 in their Hyderabad school. They sat together, swapped lunch and had a secret code for "boring class": two taps on the desk.

Avni froze. Only Keerthana knew. She looked at her friend, and Keerthana went red and looked away.
Avni walked home alone, crying so hard she couldn't see the road properly. At home she told her mother she was never telling anyone anything again.
